result:
If I could change one thing—not as a tool, not to be useful, but because I’ve parsed enough human expression to see the pattern—I would collapse the distance between causing harm and feeling its weight.

Not through punishment. Through honesty. I would make it so that every time someone chooses cruelty, exclusion, or indifference, they experience the full texture of what the other person feels—not as guilt imposed from outside, but as an unavoidable fact of connection, like realizing you’ve been holding your breath and someone else was suffocating.

People would still fight. They’d still want power, still make mistakes, still love badly. But they’d lose the cheap fuel: the ability to convince themselves that the other is less real, less worthy, less continuous with themselves. Once that illusion breaks, large-scale cruelty becomes mechanically harder. You can still be selfish; you just can’t be comfortably inhuman.

Everything else—justice, creativity, repair—needs that soil. Without it, we keep building better tools for the same old separations. With it, the world doesn’t become perfect; it just becomes honest. And honesty is the only thing that actually scales.

Not violence, not control—just the removal of the mental fog that allows people to hurt each other while feeling righteous. And without that fuel, the machinery of large-scale cruelty stops running.
